stories.headline: Update: America Marks 250th Birthday With Storms, Heat, White Supremacist March, and Trump's National Mall Speech
stories.summary:
The United States celebrated its 250th anniversary of independence Saturday with a wave of events across the country, but the day was marked by severe disruptions. A dangerous heat dome gripping the eastern United States forced the cancellation of Washington's Independence Day parade, while a severe thunderstorm prompted evacuation of crowds gathered on the National Mall ahead of President Trump's highly anticipated speech. Trump ultimately vowed to deliver the address regardless of the hour, posting that he would "wait it out" until conditions allowed.

President Trump delivered the centerpiece address on the National Mall before a fireworks display billed as the largest in U.S. history. The speech followed an eve appearance at Mount Rushmore in which Trump warned of a 'communist menace' and tied his rhetoric to immigration ahead of November midterms — a departure from the traditionally unifying tone presidents have adopted at national commemorative events. The White House also unveiled Trump-signed commemorative dollar bills and launched 'Trump Accounts,' a children's savings program authorized by congressional Republicans.

Hundreds of masked members of the white supremacist organization Patriot Front marched through Washington's Capitol Hill neighborhood near Union Station on Saturday afternoon, chanting slogans including 'Reclaim America.' The group, led by founder Thomas Rousseau, carried Confederate flags and wore matching khakis and white face coverings. The march drew condemnation and added to the day's charged atmosphere as the nation grappled with a politically divided semiquincentennial.

Former Presidents Biden, Obama, Bush, and Clinton each issued messages emphasizing the United States as a 'constant work in progress,' offering an implicit contrast to the current political climate. Pope Leo XIV addressed Americans from Lampedusa, praising the country's history of welcoming migrants and urging it to live up to the ideals of the Declaration of Independence. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu also announced Saturday that he and Trump had agreed to meet at the White House in the coming week.

stories.headline: Hungary's New Government Files Constitutional Bill to Remove Orban-Allied President
stories.summary:
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government has introduced a constitutional amendment aimed at removing the president, an ally of former nationalist leader Viktor Orban, and rolling back Orban's broader political influence. The filing marks one of the most direct legislative moves yet by Magyar's administration to dismantle the institutional architecture that Orban built over more than a decade in power.

Magyar, who rose to prominence as a Orban critic before leading his party to a surprise electoral victory, has made reversing democratic backsliding a central plank of his government. The constitutional bill represents a significant escalation in that effort, targeting the presidency — a position that Orban allies have used to exercise continued influence despite losing government control.

The move is likely to trigger a major political and legal battle in Budapest, as Orban's Fidesz party retains substantial representation in parliament and has used constitutional mechanisms in the past to protect its institutional positions. Hungary's situation is being closely watched by the European Union, which suspended billions in funds over rule-of-law concerns during the Orban era and is now navigating the question of how quickly to restore ties with the Magyar government.

stories.headline: French Aircraft Carrier Charles de Gaulle Withdraws From Hormuz After U.S.-Iran Interim Deal
stories.summary:
France's flagship aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle is returning to its home port after nearly two months deployed near the Strait of Hormuz, as an interim peace agreement between the United States and Iran reduces tensions in the strategically vital waterway. The withdrawal marks a visible de-escalation of Western military presence in the region following months of heightened confrontation.

The de Gaulle's departure comes as Iran has simultaneously announced preferential transit terms for China and other allied nations using the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran's ambassador to Beijing confirming that 'friendly nations' will receive special consideration on service fees. Together, the developments signal a reshaping of geopolitical alignments around one of the world's most critical chokepoints, through which roughly 20 percent of global oil supply passes.

Washington Examiner chief political correspondent Byron York noted Saturday that it has remained difficult to see measurable traction in U.S.-Iran negotiations, despite the 60-day ceasefire extension secured in June. The convergence of Iran's China concessions and the French carrier withdrawal underscores the complex and still-fluid diplomatic landscape in the Persian Gulf region.

stories.headline: Serena Williams Withdraws From Wimbledon Doubles Due to Knee Injury, Ending Comeback Bid
stories.summary:
Serena Williams has pulled out of her planned Wimbledon doubles appearance with sister Venus Williams because of a knee injury, ending the most anticipated element of her tennis comeback. The 44-year-old, a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion, sustained the knee problem during her singles loss to Australia's Maya Joint on Tuesday, with the joint swelling rapidly after she left the court.

The Williams sisters, six-time Wimbledon doubles champions together, had been scheduled to play Colombia's Camila Osorio and Argentina's Solana Sierra on Saturday in what would have been their first Grand Slam doubles appearance since 2022. Williams shared photographs on Instagram of knee bandaging and syringes used to drain fluid, and said she was 'heartbroken' to withdraw. 'Coming back to compete again has been a gift,' she wrote, adding 'stay tuned to a city near you.'

Williams has not confirmed the next step in her comeback. The tennis calendar shifts to the North American hard court season, culminating at the U.S. Open in late August and September — the site of what many believed was her retirement match in 2022. Williams turns 45 in September and is a six-time singles champion at Flushing Meadows.

stories.headline: Paul Pelosi, 86, Faces Hit-and-Run Charge After Striking Parked Car in Napa County
stories.summary:
Paul Pelosi, husband of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, is facing a misdemeanor hit-and-run charge after the Napa County Sheriff's Office says he struck an unoccupied parked vehicle in Yountville, California, on Friday and drove away before his own car became disabled and blocked a nearby road. Deputies identified Pelosi as the driver and he allegedly told investigators he knew he had hit something but did not know what it was.

Authorities said alcohol was ruled out as a factor, with a preliminary alcohol screening device registering 0.00. Pelosi was not arrested at the scene, which the sheriff's office described as standard procedure for this class of misdemeanor. The case will be referred to the Napa County District Attorney's Office for review, and a driver re-evaluation referral will be submitted to the California DMV — a common measure taken with elderly drivers.

The incident marks the second driving-related legal matter for Pelosi in Napa County in recent years. In 2022, he pleaded guilty to misdemeanor drunk driving causing injury following a separate crash and was sentenced to three years of probation, five days in jail, a DUI education program, and an ignition interlock device requirement.

stories.headline: Joey Chestnut Wins 18th Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest with 66 Hot Dogs
stories.summary:
Joey Chestnut claimed his 18th Nathan's Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest title on Friday at Coney Island, consuming 66 hot dogs and buns to defeat the field in the annual July 4th tradition. It marked Chestnut's 10th consecutive victory in contests he has entered, following his absence from the 2024 event due to a sponsorship dispute with Major League Eating.

Chestnut was neck-and-neck with 2024 champion Patrick Bertoletti and James Webb through the early stages before pulling away decisively at the midpoint, reaching 42 hot dogs by the three-minute mark with a 10-wiener lead. He acknowledged he fell short of his personal record of 76, citing heat and fatigue in near-triple-digit temperatures. Miki Sudo won the women's competition with 39 hot dogs and buns, extending her unbeaten record in every Nathan's contest she has entered since 2014.

Chestnut competed while serving a 180-day probation sentence after pleading guilty to a misdemeanor battery charge stemming from an unrelated incident earlier this year; he was granted permission to travel to New York for the event.

stories.headline: AfD Reelects Leaders at Convention as Tens of Thousands Protest in Erfurt
stories.summary:
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party held its national convention Saturday in Erfurt, overwhelmingly reelecting co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla to two-year terms. Weidel received 81% of the delegate vote and Chrupalla 70%, both running unopposed, as the party sought to project unity ahead of what Weidel called a "year of destiny."

Tens of thousands of protesters surrounded the convention hall, with police reporting roughly 31,000 participants in Saturday's rallies. The demonstrations were largely peaceful, though some protesters clashed with police. Critics also noted the convention coincided with the 100th anniversary of a nearby Nazi Party gathering that consolidated Adolf Hitler's power — symbolism the AfD dismissed as irrelevant.

The AfD has risen from second place in February 2025's national election, where it won 20.8% of the vote — the best far-right result since World War II — to first place in current polls. Mainstream German parties maintain a stated "firewall" policy of refusing coalition partnerships with the AfD, though calls from some quarters to ban the party outright have not cleared Germany's high constitutional bar for party prohibition.

The convention reflects a broader tension inside Germany over how to respond to a party that is simultaneously the country's most popular and its most controversial political force. Supporters argue the AfD represents legitimate grievances over immigration and economic policy; opponents say its rhetoric and leadership echo dangerous historical precedents.

stories.headline: University of Minnesota Scientists Build Most Life-Like Synthetic Cell Yet, Capable of Growth and Division
stories.summary:
Researchers at the University of Minnesota have created what they describe as the most life-like synthetic cell ever assembled from nonliving components, a system they call "SpudCell." Unlike prior efforts that began with living organisms, SpudCell was built from chemically defined, nonliving parts and carries a 90,000-base-pair genome that enables it to produce proteins, replicate DNA, grow, and divide into daughter cells under controlled laboratory conditions.

The researchers also demonstrated a rudimentary form of natural selection: after introducing a genetic mutation that allowed some cells to grow faster than others, the faster-growing variants produced more offspring and became increasingly prevalent over successive generations. The team said the work represents "key milestones towards construction of synthetic life" and could eventually underpin biotechnology applications involving fully artificial organisms.

Significant limitations remain. SpudCell cannot survive outside carefully maintained laboratory environments, requires externally supplied nutrients and specialized components, and depends on ribosomes purified from E. coli bacteria. After five generations, only about 30% of daughter cells inherited the complete synthetic genome. The findings were published Thursday as a preprint on bioRxiv and have not yet undergone peer review.

The work raises both scientific excitement and ethical questions about the boundary between chemistry and life. The researchers acknowledged their system remains far less capable than even the simplest naturally occurring living cells, but said the demonstration of a complete synthetic cell cycle — growth, DNA replication, and division linked to heritable traits — is a milestone the field has been pursuing for decades.

stories.headline: Putin Faces Rare Domestic Criticism Over Ukraine War Costs, Fuel Shortages, and Mounting Casualties
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is confronting an unusual level of public criticism at home as the cumulative toll of more than four years of war in Ukraine strains the country's economy and social fabric. Prominent figures inside Russia are increasingly attributing fuel shortages, rising inflation, and mounting battlefield casualties to the conduct of the war — a significant shift in a country where open criticism of the conflict has carried severe legal risk.

Ukraine's intensified deep-strike campaign against Russian energy infrastructure has contributed to the domestic pressure, with high-profile attacks on fuel depots and oil terminals drawing attention inside Russia to the war's material costs. Putin publicly dismissed Ukraine's recent military gains as "imaginary achievements," calling its leaders "play actors," in remarks that analysts read as an attempt to push back against a growing sense that the war is not proceeding as Moscow had promised.

The criticism remains constrained compared to what would be seen in open societies, and there is no sign of organized political opposition capable of challenging Putin's hold on power. Nevertheless, observers note that the willingness of prominent Russian voices to assign blame to Kremlin decision-making represents a meaningful departure from the enforced consensus that has characterized public discourse since the invasion began in February 2022.

The development comes as Ukraine continues long-range strikes on Russian territory and as Western support for Kyiv remains a contested issue ahead of ongoing NATO discussions. The domestic pressure on Putin could influence Russian negotiating posture, though analysts caution that authoritarian systems can absorb significant internal strain before it translates into policy change.

stories.headline: 'Flamingo Revolution' Protests Intensify in Albania, Thousands Demand PM's Resignation
stories.summary:
Tens of thousands of Albanians have taken to the streets in nightly rallies demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, with protests that began over an environmental dispute now expanding into a broader movement against governance, corruption, and inequality. The demonstrations were initially sparked by plans for a luxury resort development near Narta Lagoon — a protected wetland habitat — in which investors including Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump, hold an interest. The government has granted the development "special investor" status despite no planning permission having been issued.

The protests escalated sharply after video spread online showing private security guards beating a demonstrator at the development site, an incident confirmed by Rama himself. Crowds have since broadened their grievances to include schools, hospitals, infrastructure, and what critics describe as a governing style beholden to oligarchs and organized crime.

Rama, whose Socialist Party has held power for 13 years, has characterized the protests as a sign of healthy democracy and defended his record, pointing to Albania's significant economic growth, tourism boom, and progress toward EU membership. Prominent dissident intellectual Fatos Lubonja, who spent 17 years in a communist-era labor camp, countered that the current government is propped up by "oligarchs, organised crime, the media and corrupt internationals."

The protests represent a significant political challenge for Rama at a sensitive moment, as Albania is on course to complete EU accession negotiations by the end of next year — one of the fastest trajectories among Western Balkan nations.

stories.headline: Three Children Die After Boat Capsizes on Geneva Lake in Wisconsin During Severe Storm
stories.summary:
Three children were killed on Friday after a recreational boat carrying six adults and four children capsized on Geneva Lake in Wisconsin during a sudden and severe storm. The Geneva Lake Law Enforcement Agency said the vessel was overwhelmed by high winds and waves as it attempted to navigate to safety, ultimately taking on water, capsizing, and sinking. All six adults and one child were rescued; the three remaining children were found after an intensive search but could not be revived despite lifesaving efforts at the scene and by EMTs.

Officials said all four children on board were wearing life jackets at the time of the capsizing. The victims, believed to all be under the age of 13, have not been formally identified pending family notification. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and the Geneva Lake Law Enforcement Agency have opened an investigation into the circumstances of the sinking.

Authorities used the incident to issue a public safety warning ahead of the July 4th holiday weekend, urging boaters to closely monitor weather forecasts and seek harbor immediately when threatening conditions develop.

stories.headline: India's West Bengal Drops Eggs From School Lunches in Favor of Vegetarian Meals, Sparking Nutrition Debate
stories.summary:
India's West Bengal state government has announced it will replace eggs in some government school lunch programs with vegetarian alternatives, handing meal preparation to the Annamrita Foundation — the food service arm of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON), better known as the Hare Krishna movement. The move by the newly elected Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government has ignited a nationwide debate over the intersection of religion, nutrition policy, and the rights of India's poorest children.

For millions of underprivileged students, the midday meal program is the most nutritious — and sometimes only — meal they receive each day. Nutrition campaigners argue that eggs are among the cheapest and most effective protein sources available, costing roughly eight rupees (about eight U.S. cents) each, and that any replacement risks harming child development. The opposition All India Trinamool Congress, which governed West Bengal until May, has accused the BJP of trying to "impose vegetarianism" on schoolchildren for ideological reasons rooted in Hindu nationalist politics.

Defenders of the change, including Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, say the program aims to provide children with "good and pure food" and deny that the decision is religiously motivated. ISKCON has pushed back on criticism, noting it runs one of the world's largest school meal operations through the Akshaya Patra Foundation. The organization says carefully planned vegetarian alternatives such as soybeans and kidney beans can match the nutritional value of eggs.

The project has not yet formally begun, and ISKCON told the BBC that discussions are still ongoing. However, the episode has reignited a recurring controversy in India, where several BJP-governed states have previously attempted to reduce or remove eggs from school menus, drawing repeated protests from health advocates and opposition politicians.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Major Oil Terminal and Naval Base Near St. Petersburg
stories.summary:
Ukraine launched a large-scale drone assault on Russia's second-largest city overnight, striking a major oil terminal in St. Petersburg and a key Russian Baltic Fleet naval base at Kronstadt, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced Saturday. St. Petersburg Governor Aleksandr Beglov confirmed the oil terminal was hit, saying 72 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the city and surrounding Leningrad region, and urged residents to stay indoors. No casualties were reported.

The terminal is described by Ukraine's military as one of Russia's largest, capable of producing 12.5 million tonnes of petroleum products annually. Kyiv says the strikes were aimed at infrastructure generating revenue for Russia's war effort. Ukraine has claimed it has disabled nearly 43 percent of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent strikes — a figure that has not been independently verified.

The attack came as Russia's President Vladimir Putin faces rare domestic criticism over fuel shortages, rising inflation, and mounting military casualties tied to the prolonged conflict. In a separate development Saturday, Ukraine's military denied Russian claims that the key eastern town of Kostyantynivka had fallen to Russian forces, with a military spokesman saying Ukrainian forces retained control though acknowledging small Russian infantry groups had infiltrated combat positions.

The strikes mark a significant escalation in Ukraine's long-range campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, with targets now reaching approximately 850 kilometers from Ukraine's border. Russia had not publicly commented on the Kronstadt naval base claim as of Saturday morning.

stories.headline: Keiko Fujimori Declared Winner of Peru's Presidential Election
stories.summary:
Peru's electoral court has certified right-wing candidate Keiko Fujimori as the winner of the country's June 7 presidential runoff, nearly a month after voting took place. Fujimori won with 50.135 percent of the vote compared to 49.865 percent for left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez — a margin of fewer than 50,000 votes. It is her fourth attempt at the presidency; she will be sworn in on July 28 and will become the nation's ninth president in a decade.

Fujimori, 57, ran on a platform of cracking down on organized crime, which has soared in Peru in recent years, and attracting private investment for economic growth. She leaned on the controversial legacy of her father, former President Alberto Fujimori, who was jailed for crimes against humanity including extrajudicial killings and forced sterilizations during his authoritarian rule.

Sánchez, a former foreign trade minister, has alleged the runoff was "seriously compromised" and cited strong Fujimori support among Peruvians abroad as evidence of irregularities. His party filed an appeal Saturday calling for the result to be nullified, though electoral courts had certified the outcome.

Fujimori's election continues a regional trend: alongside Colombia's newly elected President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, her win marks a broader rightward shift in Latin American politics, following leaders in El Salvador, Ecuador, and Argentina who have aligned themselves with U.S. President Donald Trump.

stories.headline: Iran Offers China and Allies Preferential Terms for Strait of Hormuz Transit
stories.summary:
Iran's ambassador to China said Saturday that Beijing and other nations deemed friendly to Tehran will receive "special considerations" when Iran sets fees for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The announcement signals a dramatic shift from the pre-war status quo, when vessels passed through the strategically vital waterway without paying any toll.

The Hormuz strait is one of the world's most critical oil chokepoints, through which roughly 20 percent of global petroleum supplies pass. Iran's move to monetize transit access — and to tiered it based on geopolitical alignment — could have significant implications for global energy markets and for nations, including European countries and Japan, that are not among Tehran's preferred partners.

The announcement came as U.S.-Iran talks in Qatar over Hormuz tensions are reported to be continuing. Granting China preferential access could deepen economic ties between Tehran and Beijing while increasing pressure on Western nations dependent on the strait for energy imports.

Details on the structure, timing, or magnitude of proposed fees were not disclosed. The move is likely to draw sharp reactions from the United States and its allies, who have long opposed any Iranian effort to control or restrict commercial traffic through the strait.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV Visits Lampedusa, Calls on Europe to Do More for Migrants
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV traveled to the Italian island of Lampedusa on Saturday, visiting graves of migrants who died crossing the Mediterranean and urging European leaders to take greater responsibility for the migration crisis. Speaking at a mass on the island, the pontiff declared that "those who have lost their lives in this sea are victims both of decisions that were made and of decisions that were not made."

Lampedusa, located roughly 90 miles off Tunisia's coast, is a primary entry point for migrants crossing from Africa to Europe and home to an overcrowded reception center. More than 1,400 people have died or gone missing in Mediterranean crossings this year, including 28 children, according to the UN's International Organization for Migration.

The visit comes two weeks after the European Union approved tougher migration rules allowing stricter border controls and broader detention powers — measures that reflect a broader hardening of migration policy across the continent. Pope Leo, who has made support for migrants a central theme of his papacy since taking office in May 2025, called on Europe to develop a "long-term strategic plan" for receiving and integrating migrants while addressing conditions in their countries of origin.

The pope's stance puts him at continuing odds with a number of Western leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, who have pursued restrictive immigration policies. Supporters of tighter border controls argue that robust enforcement is necessary to manage migration flows and protect national security, while critics say hardened policies leave vulnerable populations in dangerous conditions.

stories.headline: Trump Delivers Politically Charged Independence Day Speech at Mount Rushmore
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump marked America's 250th anniversary with a speech at Mount Rushmore on Friday that began with themes of American exceptionalism before pivoting to sharp partisan warnings, declaring communism a greater threat to the United States than World War I, World War II, Pearl Harbor, or 9/11. The speech drew immediate comparisons to the Red Scare of the 1950s, departing sharply from the traditionally apolitical, unifying tone of Independence Day addresses delivered by past presidents at major national commemorations.

The address came amid a brutal heat wave that forced the temporary closure of the Great American State Fair on the National Mall, canceled Philadelphia's Salute to Independence parade, and disrupted festivities across the eastern United States. Officials urged celebrants to stay hydrated and seek air-conditioned spaces throughout the holiday weekend.

Supporters of the president praised his willingness to name what they see as genuine ideological threats to American freedom, while critics argued the speech exploited a unifying national anniversary for partisan purposes. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, delivered a counter-address framing America as a nation of contradictions striving toward its founding ideals.

Trump has also drawn attention for his expressed desire to have his likeness added to Mount Rushmore alongside Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln — a proposal that has generated both enthusiastic support among his backers and sharp opposition from historians and Native American tribes who consider the monument itself contested.

stories.headline: Polish PM Warns of 'Critical' Months Ahead After U.S. Intelligence Reports Russian Plot to Attack Poland
stories.summary:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk issued a public warning Friday that the coming months could be "critical" for Poland and NATO allies in the Baltic region, citing U.S. intelligence reports indicating Russia may be planning an armed provocation on Polish soil. Tusk said Poland was preparing for "various scenarios" and urged citizens not to panic while acknowledging the threats were serious enough to warrant attention.

Polish news outlet Onet reported that sources close to President Karol Nawrocki said Washington had issued multiple specific warnings to Warsaw about a plot targeting Polish infrastructure with missiles, drones, or troops. The purported Russian plan, also reported by Britain's Daily Telegraph, would aim to pressure Ukraine's Western allies into suspending military aid to Kyiv. The White House and State Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The warnings come ahead of a NATO summit in Turkey next week, where Secretary General Mark Rutte is expected to highlight European allies' increased defense spending in response to U.S. pressure. Lithuanian and Latvian intelligence services have separately warned in recent weeks about Russian military provocations in the Baltic region, though analysts note Moscow is more likely to employ hybrid tactics such as drone incursions than a conventional attack.

Tusk told the Financial Times in April that a Russian attack on a NATO member could come within months, and his Deputy Prime Minister Radek Sikorski said in June he could not rule out a Russian "false flag" operation within two years. NATO's Article 5 mutual defense clause means any confirmed armed attack on Poland would obligate all 32 alliance members to respond.

stories.headline: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce Marry at Madison Square Garden
stories.summary:
Pop superstar Taylor Swift and NFL tight end Travis Kelce were married Friday at New York's Madison Square Garden, culminating months of intense public speculation about the closely guarded event. The 20,000-seat arena was transformed for the ceremony, though many details — including Swift's Dior wedding gown and the full guest list — remained under wraps as of Friday evening.

The wedding is among the most high-profile celebrity events in recent memory, drawing wall-to-wall media coverage and crowds of fans to the streets surrounding the venue in midtown Manhattan. The couple, who began dating in 2023, have been one of the most scrutinized pairs in American popular culture, with their relationship frequently intersecting with both the NFL season and Swift's record-breaking Eras Tour.

The event drew coverage from virtually every major national outlet. No further details about the ceremony or reception were immediately available as the couple and guests continued private celebrations.

stories.headline: Ukrainian Suspect Sought After Parcel Bomb Injures Sanctioned Billionaire and Family in Monaco
stories.summary:
Monaco authorities are hunting a Ukrainian woman identified as the prime suspect in a parcel bombing Monday evening that left a sanctioned Ukrainian multi-millionaire, his partner, and his 13-year-old son seriously injured. Anastasiia Berezovska, 39, is believed to have left an explosive package in the entrance of an apartment building before fleeing on foot and then driving through Italy to Germany, according to Monaco's deputy prosecutor.

An Interpol Red Notice has been issued for Berezovska, who speaks German and is wanted for attempted murder, placing an explosive device on a public road, and criminal conspiracy. German special forces searched her rented apartment in the Main-Taunus district of Hesse on Thursday, seizing a vehicle she had used, but she remained at large as of Friday.

The reported target, real estate developer Vadym Yermolaiev, 58, has been living in Monaco and is subject to sanctions. Investigators said Berezovska had spent several days surveilling the residence before the attack and was caught on CCTV wearing a dark bucket hat. Authorities are also investigating possible accomplices.

Prince Albert II of Monaco called the incident a "heinous crime." The bombing adds to a pattern of targeted violence connected to Ukrainian and Russian oligarchic networks operating in Western Europe, raising questions about the reach of wartime intelligence and criminal operations into neutral third countries.
